body.text: At 8:30 a.m. on November 19, phones across South Korea rang at the same moment. The government had sent an emergency alert of the highest level – an alert that users cannot switch off. By doing so, officials wanted to find phones that test-takers had not handed in. According to local news reports in South Korea, an exam had never before set off phones nationwide.
The exam in question was the “Suneung,” the College Scholastic Ability Test. About 550,000 students were expected to sit it this year.

The Education Ministry said on November 20 that 111 cases of alleged cheating with electronic devices had been detected during the test. Three alerts went out during the day and they exposed 54 of the cases. Five test-takers used smart devices during the exam; one of them wore smart glasses.

Authorities had prepared for such devices. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced on November 17 that about 8,400 extra staff would join the roughly 75,000 proctors at 1,312 test centers. Under the plan, proctors would inspect eyeglasses and clothing for hidden devices and put stickers over buttons.

Before scores come out on December 11, an Education Ministry committee will decide penalties for all 111 cases. The government plans criminal complaints against those who used smart devices to cheat; police have opened investigations into two of the five cases already. The charge of obstructing official duties by deception carries a sentence of up to five years in prison.

Additional penalties are being explored as well. The government and the ruling Democratic Party want to extend the ban on taking the exam from one year to 10 years for those caught cheating with smart devices, and to apply it retroactively to the exam this year. For anyone who entered a university through cheating, admission could be revoked. Test-takers who are already enrolled at a university could face expulsion.

The new strict measures trace back to a confession made four days before the exam. On November 15, a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok admitted that he had cheated on the national exam for tax accountants after finishing first. He answered almost every tax law question correctly, although the average score on that section was 30.18 out of 100.

According to Han’s confession, he used a miniature camera and a smartphone to get answers from artificial intelligence (AI). He surrendered to police, and also admitted to cheating on a certified public accountant exam. The state agency in charge of the tax accountant exam began steps to cancel his passing status and announced a review of other national exams.

Public doubt then turned to other exceptional results. Lee Jin-woo, who was a 32-year-old dental student at Seoul National University, had achieved a perfect score this year on the law school entrance exam, known as the Legal Education Eligibility Test. Among law experts, it’s long been believed that it’s impossible to reach a perfect score on the test.

According to local news reports in South Korea, Lee had earned low grades on the Suneung for the 2013 academic year and entered Korea University through the exam for the 2024 academic year. He received the top grade in every subject on the exam for the 2026 academic year and moved to Seoul National University. Doubts began with an unusually clean exam booklet that he showed on YouTube.

In this context, the doubts over Lee’s capability snowballed, leading him to promise to answer the doubts by solving questions for the Suneung in public on November 19. However, he did not appear at the planned session. Later that day, police found him dead in Seoul.

The police said they would keep investigating complaints against him. As of writing, no cheating by Lee has been confirmed. The truth may never fully emerge because a deceased suspect cannot be prosecuted under South Korean law.
Whatever the truth about Lee, the events of the past week have left South Korea with deep-seated questions about testing in the age of AI and smart devices.

Exams carry unusual weight in South Korea. Many South Korean children begin cram school as early as elementary school. The university a person graduates from tends to stand in for the ability of that person. That is why a fair exam matters so much.

Now, the foundation of fair admissions has cracked. The Suneung has been the fairest route into university because every student sits for the same test on the same day. A single sitting each year is harsh for students and some have called for more chances, pointing to the frequency of the SAT in the U.S. In public debate, however, the fairness of the sitting itself had never been the issue.

Fairness had been in question for early admission. Universities plan to fill 80.3 percent of seats for the 2027 academic year through that route. It rests on school grades and student records over the course of high school. Because of this system, some argued that it favors families able to pay for private tutoring. Regular admission relies on Suneung scores and covers 19.7 percent of seats nationwide but a larger share at the top universities.

AI cheating breaks the promise on which regular admission depends. Every score is supposed to reflect the effort of the student, but Han Won-seok passed a national exam in front of proctors who noticed nothing. Online suspicion unmasked him, and it led to the series of suspicions that earlier cheaters might have similarly gone undetected during the test. Some of them already hold places at top universities and in licensed professions. The government cannot realistically find every one of them.

Early admission, although it draws from a longer student record, is not immune to AI risk, because students can use AI to complete their school coursework. On the other hand, honest test-takers will have to carry the heightened suspicion that falls on every high score.

Beyond national exam, the same doubt has reached university classrooms. Korea University voided the midterm of an online course in October 2025 after students shared answers in chat rooms. Also in the fall of 2025, Seoul National University ordered a retest for one class section after cheating was detected. The classroom has changed, but the rules for grading have not.

In order to soothe the public’s concerns and suspicions on the fairness of the tests, the government has met these social changes with stepped-up enforcement. At a meeting with senior aides at the presidential office in Seoul, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for a total overhaul of the national exam system.

“Do not skimp on administrative resources or funding,” Lee said during the meeting on November 20. In his view, traditional exam management cannot match AI-assisted cheating. Officials were told to work with AI companies and to investigate cheating on past exams.

The prime minister, Han Seong-sook, took the same line. At Government Complex Seoul that day, Han chaired the first meeting of a task force on cheating and promised to search for cheating missed by proctors.

Rewards for informers are part of that approach. In a post on X on November 21, Lee rejected earlier government descriptions of the reward as a maximum of 100 million won per case. As a rule, the reward is a minimum that rises with the number of cheaters. A self-reporting cheater who names partners would still get the full reward and a lighter punishment. He called exam cheating as serious a crime as corruption by public officials and promised to track offenders to the end and to build defenses against high-tech cheating.

Last weekend, 14 universities scheduled essay exams, which is one of the key grading criteria for those who applied for early admissions. Applicants were caught with AI-enabled smart glasses at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul in October. Two days before its exam, Sungkyunkwan University told applicants to use only writing instruments supplied by the university. The Korean Council for University Education said universities would apply the same strict principles to cheating at their own exams.

On November 22, Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned from the post to take the responsibility for the turmoil caused by the inadequate response of his ministry to the cheating scandal. Lee announced the reshuffle of his Cabinet members on November 23, excluding the post of Education Minister.

If policy does not keep pace with technology, abusers of the technology will benefit. Despite the government’s clear warnings for disadvantages and punishment toward those who attempt to cheat, someone will take advantage to get admitted to the top school by using AI – and they may get away with it.

However, a search for ways to test people without AI throws up its own complications. It’s difficult, if not impossible, to block AI use entirely. In addition, a student who eschews AI in school and university may fall behind in the real world. In South Korea, AI use is pervasive across the workforce, and only poised to grow as the technology advances.
Until these questions are resolved, doubt will continue to cloud South Korea’s exams.
